discovery: Theory of defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the prediction of the hexatic phase

nominees.name: A. Peter Young
nominees.affiliation: University of California, Santa Cruz, USA

subfield: Condensed matter physics: topological defects, broken symmetry and soft matter
motivation: The 2016 Prize recognized Kosterlitz and Thouless for topological phase transitions, but the full story of two-dimensional crystals was completed by Halperin, Nelson and Young (1978-79). They showed that a 2D solid melts in two steps: dislocation unbinding first destroys translational order and leaves a new phase of matter, the hexatic, which keeps quasi-long-range bond-orientational order. The hexatic then melts through the unbinding of disclinations. This prediction of an entirely new state of matter, based purely on topology and broken symmetry, has been confirmed quantitatively in colloidal monolayers, freely suspended liquid-crystal films, electrons on helium and hard-disk simulations. The theory, together with Nelson's work on bond-orientational order, now underlies how we understand order, defects and frustration in membranes, colloids, active matter and vortex lattices. It is a model of how topology turns geometry into counting. (Disclosure: Nelson was my doctoral advisor.)
